items.question:
A digital transformation lead at a logistics company has built a Claude-assisted shipment exception workflow. After six months in production, an internal audit finds two problems: (1) during two 3-hour Claude outages last quarter, 140 shipment exceptions were not processed, causing customer SLA breaches; (2) the audit cannot determine who reviewed and approved exceptions resolved during normal operations, because the approval log captures only the exception ID and resolution code, not the reviewer's identity.

Which single action MOST efficiently addresses BOTH findings?

options.A: Add reviewer identity to the approval log and build a manual exception processing procedure for Claude outages.
options.B: Deploy a secondary Claude instance that processes exceptions when the primary is unavailable, and add reviewer identity to the approval log.
options.C: Add reviewer identity to the approval log and configure Claude to alert the team when it detects an impending outage.
options.D: Build a manual exception processing procedure for outages, and configure the approval log to capture the full exception narrative in addition to the ID and resolution code.

items.question:
A clinical trials coordinator at a CRO uses Claude to draft protocol deviation reports when study procedures are not followed as specified. The coordinator's manager proposes that minor deviations — those already categorised as non-significant in the sponsor's risk matrix — can be submitted to the sponsor without a medical monitor review.

What is the MOST appropriate response to this proposal?

options.A: Accept the proposal: non-significant deviations are by definition low-risk and do not require medical monitor review.
options.B: Accept the proposal only if the sponsor has explicitly agreed in writing that non-significant deviations can be submitted without medical monitor review.
options.C: Reject the proposal: all deviation reports submitted to a regulatory sponsor require medical monitor review regardless of the sponsor's risk categorisation.
options.D: Accept the proposal if Claude's deviation drafts achieve 95% accuracy on the first three submissions.

items.question:
A head of operations at a logistics company documents a manual fallback procedure for their Claude-assisted rate-quoting workflow. The procedure was documented six months ago but has never been tested. During a real Claude outage, the team discovers the procedure references a rate table that was superseded four months ago.

What does this incident PRIMARILY reveal about fallback procedure management?

options.A: Fallback procedures should be automated rather than manual, to remove dependency on accurate documentation.
options.B: Fallback procedures must be tested periodically and updated when any process element they reference changes, to remain actionable.
options.C: The team should have identified the superseded rate table before attempting to use the fallback procedure during the outage.
options.D: The fallback procedure was too detailed; a simpler procedure would have been less likely to contain outdated references.

items.question:
A strategy analyst at a consulting firm is preparing a market analysis for a client. She plans to feed data from a third-party market research subscription (licensed for internal use only) into Claude to generate the analysis. The client will receive the final report.

What data governance concern must be addressed BEFORE creating this workflow?

options.A: Whether Claude can accurately interpret and summarise the third-party market research data format.
options.B: Whether the third-party licence permits the data to be processed by an AI tool and whether client delivery of AI-derived analysis is within the licence scope.
options.C: Whether the client has the appropriate technology to receive an AI-generated report.
options.D: Whether the market research provider has been notified that its data will be used in conjunction with an AI tool.

items.question:
A customer experience manager at a utility company uses Claude to categorise and draft responses to customer complaints. After four weeks, the manager identifies a category of complaints Claude consistently handles poorly: complex billing disputes involving multiple overlapping tariff changes, where the customer has received inconsistent advice over several previous calls.

What is the MOST appropriate workflow design change?

options.A: Add example responses for the complex billing dispute category to Claude's Project instructions, so Claude can produce better drafts for these cases.
options.B: Classify this complaint category as an escalation trigger and route these cases directly to a senior billing specialist before Claude drafts a response.
options.C: Instruct Claude to produce a partial draft for these cases and add a note that manual completion is required.
options.D: Remove the complex billing dispute category from Claude's task scope entirely and handle them through a separate, non-AI-assisted process.

items.question:
A compliance operations manager at a broker-dealer uses Claude to draft FINRA regulatory reports from structured trade data. The current workflow submits Claude-generated reports to FINRA after the compliance officer reviews and electronically signs them. An efficiency consultant recommends removing the compliance officer's sign-off step, replacing it with an automated post-submission audit that reviews 10% of filed reports.

What is the MOST significant flaw in this recommendation?

options.A: A 10% sample is statistically insufficient to detect systematic errors in regulatory filings at volume.
options.B: Automated audits cannot replicate the compliance officer's knowledge of regulatory nuance in the report content.
options.C: Post-submission audit reviews errors after they have already been filed with the regulator; unlike a pre-submission gate, it cannot prevent a non-compliant filing from reaching FINRA.
options.D: The compliance officer's electronic signature is legally required for FINRA submissions and cannot be automated away.

items.question:
A senior manager at a Big Four accounting firm uses Claude to draft a client-facing internal audit report. She uploads the client's internal financial data and operational metrics to Claude's context. The final report is reviewed by a partner and delivered to the client. A risk officer flags that the workflow may create a data exposure risk beyond the client deliverable.

What risk is the officer MOST likely identifying?

options.A: The client may object to their data being processed by an AI tool, creating a reputational risk for the firm.
options.B: The client's internal financial data and operational metrics uploaded to Claude's context may be processed alongside other clients' data if the same Claude account or Project is used for multiple engagements.
options.C: The partner's review may not be sufficiently detailed to catch all inaccuracies in Claude's draft before client delivery.
options.D: The client's data may be retained by the AI provider beyond the engagement period, creating a data residency or retention issue.

items.question:
A head of digital operations at a retailer has built a three-component Claude-assisted workflow: a connector pulls live inventory data, Claude generates reorder recommendations, and a second connector writes approved recommendations to the purchasing system. During a network maintenance window, the inventory connector becomes unavailable. Claude generates reorder recommendations based on cached inventory data from four hours ago, which is approved and written to the purchasing system without the approver noticing the data is stale.

Which design change would MOST directly prevent this failure mode from recurring?

options.A: Add a redundant inventory data source that activates automatically when the primary connector is unavailable.
options.B: Require the inventory connector to surface a data timestamp alongside every data pull, and add a workflow rule that blocks Claude from generating recommendations if the data timestamp is older than a defined threshold.
options.C: Instruct Claude to state the data source and timestamp in its recommendation output, so the approver can assess data currency before approving.
options.D: Schedule maintenance windows outside business hours to prevent the inventory connector from being unavailable during operational hours.

items.question:
A legal operations director at a global law firm is designing a Claude-assisted workflow to screen incoming matter requests for conflicts of interest. Claude checks the matter's parties against the firm's conflict database and produces a preliminary conflict assessment. The director proposes that matters with a 'clear' Claude assessment (no conflicts found) proceed to the fee-earner immediately, while only 'uncertain' assessments go to the conflicts team.

A senior partner raises an objection. Which objection is MOST valid?

options.A: Claude may not have access to the full conflicts database if the connector is not configured correctly.
options.B: A 'clear' Claude assessment depends on the quality and completeness of the conflicts database; if the database has gaps, Claude will assess matters as clear that actually have conflicts, and these matters will proceed without conflicts team review.
options.C: Fee-earners may not trust a 'clear' assessment produced by an AI and may request conflicts team review anyway, negating the efficiency gain.
options.D: The conflicts team may become de-skilled if they only review uncertain cases and lose the ability to identify conflicts in clear-pass matters.

items.question:
An internal audit director at a regulated bank reviews the AI audit trail for a Claude-assisted loan origination workflow. She finds that the log is stored in a standard database table that allows records to be updated or deleted by database administrators. The director flags this as a deficiency.

What is the MOST accurate explanation of the deficiency?

options.A: The log should be encrypted to prevent unauthorised access to audit records containing borrower information.
options.B: Database administrators have the technical ability to modify or delete audit records, which means the log cannot provide reliable evidence of what actually occurred in the event of a dispute or regulatory examination.
options.C: The log should be stored in a separate database from the loan origination system to prevent commingling of operational and audit data.
options.D: Standard database tables do not support the query performance needed to retrieve large volumes of audit records efficiently during a regulatory examination.

items.question: A VP of operations at a mid-size insurance company is designing a Claude-assisted workflow for processing 200 new commercial property insurance applications per week. The workflow will: extract data from submitted application forms, generate a risk assessment narrative, route for underwriter review, and update the policy administration system after underwriter approval. Which TWO design decisions are MOST critical to the integrity and auditability of this workflow? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Defining the specific data fields Claude is permitted to extract from application forms, excluding any fields not required for the risk assessment.
options.B: Configuring the policy administration system update to be triggered by the underwriter's approval action, not by Claude's risk assessment generation.
options.C: Using a higher-tier model for applications above a defined commercial property value threshold, to improve reasoning depth for complex risks.
options.D: Logging each application's extracted data, Claude's risk assessment narrative, the underwriter's identity, and the approval timestamp before the policy system is updated.
options.E: Configuring Claude to regenerate the risk assessment if the narrative falls below a minimum word count, to ensure completeness.

items.question:
A service operations manager at a telecom company learns that the escalation team handling Claude-flagged complex billing disputes has a maximum capacity of 50 cases per week. Claude is currently flagging an average of 80 cases per week for escalation. The 30-case overflow is being resolved by junior agents without the escalation team's involvement.

What is the PRIMARY design problem this situation reveals?

options.A: The escalation criteria are too broad, causing Claude to over-flag cases that could be resolved without specialist involvement.
options.B: The escalation path's capacity does not match the volume of cases Claude is identifying as requiring escalation, forcing ad hoc resolution of overflow cases outside the designed control structure.
options.C: Junior agents lack the training to resolve complex billing disputes, creating a quality risk in the overflow cases.
options.D: Claude's flagging rate should be reduced by adjusting the confidence threshold to decrease the number of cases reaching the escalation team.

items.question:
A research analyst at a hedge fund uploads a 600-page due diligence document to Claude and asks for a comprehensive risk summary. Claude produces a summary, but the analyst notices that the final 150 pages of the document — covering regulatory correspondence — are not referenced anywhere in the summary.

What is the MOST likely explanation and MOST appropriate workflow design response?

options.A: Claude deprioritised the regulatory correspondence as less important than the financial sections; the prompt should ask Claude to weight all sections equally.
options.B: The document exceeded Claude's processing capacity for long inputs; the analyst should split the document and run separate analyses for each section, then synthesise the results.
options.C: Claude may have reached the effective limit of its attention on a very long document; the analyst should provide explicit instructions directing Claude to summarise the regulatory section specifically.
options.D: The regulatory correspondence should be uploaded as a separate file with its own dedicated prompt asking Claude to summarise the regulatory risks it contains.

items.question:
A head of operations at a consumer lending company is designing a Claude-assisted workflow for processing loan modification requests. The workflow design so far: (1) Claude analyses the borrower's financial data and modification request; (2) an approval gate routes Claude's output to a loan officer for review; (3) the loan officer approves or declines the modification. The head now needs to design the resilience and escalation components before the workflow goes live.

What should the head specify FIRST in this phase?

options.A: The escalation criteria that define which Claude assessments require senior loan officer review rather than standard officer review.
options.B: The manual procedure loan officers can follow to assess modification requests without Claude when the service is unavailable.
options.C: The monitoring alerts that notify the operations team when Claude's average response time exceeds acceptable thresholds.
options.D: The secondary Claude project configured to handle overflow volume during peak processing periods.

items.question:
A digital operations director at a pharmaceutical company deployed a Claude-assisted workflow for drafting regulatory correspondence six months ago. The workflow has run successfully for 500 submissions. The director proposes discontinuing the periodic quality audits of submitted correspondence because the error rate has been consistently low.

What is the MOST important reason to maintain periodic auditing?

options.A: Regulatory authorities may require evidence of ongoing quality monitoring as part of their inspection of the company's AI governance programme.
options.B: Low historical error rates do not predict future error rates if the input data characteristics, Claude's behaviour, or the regulatory requirements change.
options.C: Auditing is required to comply with the company's AI governance policy, which mandates periodic review of all AI-assisted workflows.
options.D: Discontinuing audits would reduce the team's familiarity with the workflow's output quality and their ability to detect problems when they do occur.

items.question:
A VP of compliance at a financial services firm asks: 'If a regulator audits a specific AI-assisted advisory report we produced last year, what records do we minimally need to demonstrate that appropriate human oversight occurred?'

Which set of records MOST completely satisfies the minimum requirement?

options.A: The final delivered report and the client's signed acknowledgement that they received it.
options.B: The Claude-generated draft, the identity of the human who reviewed and approved it, and the date of approval.
options.C: The final delivered report and an internal email from the approving adviser stating the report was reviewed.
options.D: The Claude-generated draft, the client's risk profile used in the session, and the prompt used to generate the report.

items.question: A chief digital officer at a 90,000-person global bank is preparing to deploy a Claude-assisted anti-money laundering (AML) alert triage workflow across 12 countries. The workflow will process 10,000 alerts per day. The CDO asks: 'What are the two most important design requirements that no regional variation should be permitted to override?' (Choose TWO)

options.A: Every alert disposition — cleared or escalated — must be recorded in the global case management system with the timestamp and the identity of the person or system that made the disposition decision.
options.B: The alert triage interface must be presented in the local language of each region to ensure analysts can review Claude's output accurately.
options.C: No alert may be marked as cleared by an automated system without a named human compliance analyst having reviewed and confirmed the disposition.
options.D: Each regional deployment must use a locally calibrated confidence threshold for Claude's risk assessment, reflecting local transaction patterns.
options.E: The escalation path for each region must be configured to reflect that region's local regulatory reporting obligations.
